Allen Roush: So, um, uh, let's see. Uh, in that same, uh, paper, right, that I'd asked about before, right, like eyes wide shut, um, uh, you suggested, I think, mixing in vision and self-supervised features, uh, to improve grounding. Um, what do you think the most ideal vision encoder for a, uh, like multimodal language model looks like if you optimize like jointly for both like language alignment and, um, uh, uh, fine-grained like visual discrimination?
reference: Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think that's exactly the, the solution I have in mind right now is just to do both, just to do,... try to build in the, the,... Yeah, I think those are the two dominant paradigms for vision pre-training right now. I would say, I would add, a, a lot of people are talking about world models right now, right? astra.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think ideally you want both, right? You want the model to understand what the image is about, to connect that with language, but also to preserve the details that the caption might not describe. Like the example we discussed, a human playing with a dog. You want to recognize that, but you also want to know where the human is, where the dog is, what their positions are relative to each other.

So mixing in self-supervised features is one way to get complementary information. But I wouldn't say that combining two types of features is necessarily the final solution. Ideally, we would have one encoder that can learn both. And again, I think the training task matters a lot. If all your supervision is captions that don't describe these details, you don't have much reason to expect the model to preserve those details. You need training signals that actually require fine-grained visual understanding.

And maybe, maybe the ideal solution goes beyond the encoder itself. As I mentioned earlier, you want the model to be able to look back at the image. Depending on the question, different parts of the image become important. If you ask what is happening, a general representation might be enough. If you ask about a small object in the corner, you want it to go back and examine that region more carefully.

So I don't think we know the best recipe yet. But I would want both richer visual representations and a way for the model to access more detail when it needs it. Yeah.

sol.text:
Yeah, I think ideally it would not compress the image into only the information that is useful for matching a caption. That objective gives you very strong semantic alignment, but it can discard spatial relationships, fine-grained textures, counts, colors—things that captions often do not mention.

So I would probably use a mixture of objectives, or even a mixture of features. You want CLIP-like features for the high-level language alignment, and then self-supervised visual features that preserve local structure and fine-grained differences. And importantly, you should keep spatial, multi-scale, perhaps higher-resolution tokens rather than forcing everything into one global representation. Then the language model should have some mechanism to query those features or look back at particular regions when the question requires it.

Whether this is one jointly trained encoder or two complementary encoders is, to me, less fundamental. The important thing is that the training data and objectives explicitly cover both capabilities. If you only train image-caption alignment, you should not expect fine-grained perception to emerge reliably. So the ideal encoder is not just language-aligned; it preserves enough of the original visual information that the downstream model can answer questions the captioning objective never taught it to care about. Yeah.

opus.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah. so I, I want to be honest that the mixing we did in that paper is more of a, of a patch than a real solution. it works, like you, you take the CLIP features and the DINOv2 features and interleave them, and you, you do recover a lot of the, the fine-grained, discrimination ability. But fundamentally, we are just, we are just admitting that neither objective alone gives us what we want, right? So in an ideal world, I don't think you would want two encoders. I, I think you would want one encoder that has been trained with both types of, of supervision, the, the language alignment part and, and some dense, self-supervised part, and, and probably that's not very hard. it's, it's, again, kind of my, my general belief, if you want the model to be good at something, put it in the training objective. so, so I, I would guess a, a fairly simple, multi-objective training would, would get you most of the way there.

and then the second thing, which I think is more, more underappreciated, is the caption data itself. so, as I said, the, the reason CLIP doesn't know left from right is that the captions don't say left or right. and, and today we can actually fix that. we can re-caption the data with, with very strong, multimodal models, and, and make the captions, describe positions, counts, orientations, states of, of objects. so the, the, the data side fix here is, is quite cheap now compared to, to five years ago. I would, I would bet more on that than on, on a new architecture for the encoder.

and, and third, scale and resolution. It's, it's kind of funny that the vision encoders we use are, are like 300 million parameters, 400 million parameters, and we, we attach them to a, a 70B language model. That, that ratio seems, seems off to me. and also the, the input resolution, we, we squeeze everything into 224 or 336 pixels and then, then wonder why the model can't read small text. So, so higher resolution, more, more tokens per image, bigger encoders, that, that's just, kind of the boring answer, but I, I think it, it, it matters.

and, and then the last thing, which is, is more of a, an interface question than an encoder question. I, I do think we want a mechanism for the, for the model to look back at the image. right now everything gets, encoded once, and then the, the language model is, is stuck with whatever the encoder gave it. if, if the encoder threw away the information, nothing downstream can, can recover it. So whether that is, is cropping and re-encoding, or, or some, some kind of attention back into the, the raw pixels, or, or just tool use, like the model, decides to zoom in. I, I think that, that direction is, is promising and, and it, it takes some of the pressure off the encoder, having to be perfect in a, in a single forward pass. Yeah.

grok.text:
Yeah. So, so in that paper, we, we found that CLIP, if you just use CLIP as the vision encoder, it, it really misses a lot of these fine-grained visual patterns. Like spatial relations, orientation, which object is on the left, those kind of CLIP-blind pairs. And, and we showed that if you mix in features from a self-supervised vision model, you can recover some of that grounding. So that part of Allen’s reading is, is right.

I, I wouldn’t say I have a complete picture of the most ideal encoder, but if you jointly optimize for language alignment and fine-grained visual discrimination, I think it has to be trained on both, not just one of them. You still need the language alignment, because that’s the interface, right? That’s how you turn the image into tokens the language model can actually use. If you throw that away, you lose the connection to the rest of the multimodal system. But CLIP-style training by itself is not enough, because the captions just don’t talk about the details you care about. They talk about what’s in the image, not where things are, not the orientation, not the small visual differences.

So the ideal thing, in my mind, is some kind of joint training, or multi-task training. Contrastive language-image alignment, plus a self-supervised visual objective that actually forces the model to look at the pixels, the layout, the fine-grained structure. Mixing the features after the fact already helps, but I think training them together, so the same encoder has to satisfy both, would be cleaner. And also, as I said earlier, once everything is already compressed into vision tokens, the language model cannot go back and look at the image. So I, I would also want the encoder to preserve more spatial information. Maybe more tokens, higher resolution, or some way for the model to re-attend to the image instead of treating the encoder as a frozen, lossy bottleneck.

But, but the, the big lesson is still the same one. If you want the model to be good at fine-grained visual discrimination, you need to train it on that. You cannot expect matching captions to give you that for free. Yeah.

gemini.text:
Yeah. Mm-hmm. I think, again, it goes back to what I said earlier: if you want the model to be good at something, you really have to train it on that. 

With standard CLIP training, because it's trained to align image representations with text captions, it learns high-level semantic concepts very well, but it misses fine-grained visual details and spatial information, because captions simply don't mention those things. And once the vision encoder turns the image into tokens, if those fine-grained details or spatial relationships aren't captured, the downstream language model can do nothing about it. 

So I think an ideal vision encoder has to balance both. You need the language alignment to connect the visual concepts to the language model's representation, but you also need self-supervised features or objectives that force the encoder to preserve dense, fine-grained visual structures and spatial information. Whether you do that by jointly training on both objectives or by mixing the features from both types of representations, the key is to ensure that the vision tokens don't discard the fine-grained visual cues before they even reach the language model. If you have both, then the model has the high-level semantic understanding from language and the necessary visual grounding to answer detailed questions.

kimi.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, that's a, that's a great question. So in that paper, what we, what we demonstrated was more like a, a quick fix, right? We, we found that if you just take the features from a self-supervised model, like DINOv2, and, and mix them with the CLIP features, either by concatenation or, or some simple interpolation, the, the downstream multimodal language model suddenly gets much better at these visual pattern questions, the grounding questions. So that, that tells you the information was there, it was just thrown away by, by CLIP training. But, I think, I would admit that's kind of a hack, right? It's, it's not the, the ideal solution. It's kind of patching two systems together, and it has, it has overhead, it has, like, alignment issues between the two feature spaces.

So, so the ideal vision encoder, if I, if I could design it from scratch, would be one that's trained, jointly, from the beginning, with both objectives. You want the, the language alignment, so that the, the features sit in the same space that the language model expects, that's what makes connection to LLMs easy. But you also want to keep the, the fine-grained information, the spatial layout, the, the small objects, the, the text in the image, like OCR, the ability to count, to tell left from right, these kind of things. And, and I'm kind of repeating myself here, but the, the way to get there is still through the training objective and the training data. The reason CLIP loses this information is that the captions just don't describe it, so the contrastive objective has no pressure to keep it. Self-supervised objectives, like, like masked reconstruction, or the DINO-style self-distillation, they force the encoder to, to retain the, the low-level visual details. So I think a native encoder trained with, with both kinds of losses on, on web-scale image-text pairs, at high enough resolution, with, with native handling of different aspect ratios, that would be, that would be much closer to ideal.

And, and I think there's, there's one more thing. which is, I would want the encoder to, to not decide too early what's important. Right now, a lot of information is compressed away before the language model even sees the image, and the language model can do nothing about it. So ideally the, the encoding preserves enough, enough detail, maybe through more tokens, or, or some compression that can be expanded on demand, so that when the, the question requires fine-grained detail, the model can, can kind of go back and, and look more carefully. Of course, all of this trades off with compute, right? More tokens, higher resolution, it all costs more. So, so practically, I, I do think the, the mixture approach is still very reasonable today. But the, the jointly trained native encoder is, is probably the cleaner end goal, and I think people are, are moving in that direction. Yeah.

fable.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, that's a good question. So, so in that paper, what we did was, was kind of a, a simple fix, right? We, we take the CLIP features and the DINOv2 features, the self-supervised features, and we, we mix them together, either concatenate or, or interleave them as vision tokens for the language model. And that helped, on, on the MMVP benchmark, on these, these CLIP-blind pairs. But I, I don't think that's the ideal solution. It's, it's more of a diagnosis, like, it tells us the information is there in the pixels, the self-supervised model can see it, it's just the CLIP encoder, threw it away because the, the caption never asked for it, right?

So, if you ask me what the ideal encoder looks like, I, I would go back to my, my same answer. It's, it's less about the architecture of the encoder, it's more about what objective, what data you train it on. The, the problem with CLIP is the, the contrastive objective goes through language as a bottleneck. Whatever the caption doesn't mention, the encoder has no reason to keep. So the position, the orientation, the count, small text, these, these fine-grained things, they, they just get compressed away. self-supervised objectives like DINO, they, they don't go through language, so they, they preserve much more of the, the visual detail, but then they, they don't know what a, what a concept means, they're not aligned with, with words.

So the ideal one, I think, is, is trained with both, both kinds of supervision at the same time. You want the language supervision for the semantics, and you want some, some kind of, reconstruction or self-supervised objective so the encoder is, is forced not to throw information away. And, and then ideally you also, you don't freeze it. Like, right now, a lot of pipelines just take a frozen CLIP and plug it in. I think the encoder should be trained, together with the language model, end to end, on, on the actual tasks you care about, spatial questions, counting, OCR, all of it. If you want the model to be good at, at left versus right, you need left versus right in the training data. Again, it, it's the same lesson.

And, and the last thing, this goes back to what I said earlier, I think we need some mechanism for the model to, to look back at the image. Right now everything is, is encoded once, into a fixed number of tokens, and if, if the detail is not there, the language model can, can do nothing. So maybe the encoder should be, be less of a fixed compressor and more of a, like, on-demand thing, where the model can, can re-encode a region at higher resolution when it needs to. Whether that's, that's an architecture change or, or just a, a data and training recipe change, I, I'm not sure yet, but I, I'd guess most of the gain comes from the, the data side. Yeah.
